analysis.one_liner: Certifies subprime mortgage lenders, bans hidden fees, and outlaws forced arbitration in consumer contracts.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: after its subcommittee referral on April 15, 2002, no vote was ever taken before the Congress ended on January 3, 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required anyone making or brokering subprime mortgages to be federally trained and certified, barred high-cost lenders from charging fees not disclosed up front, made unfair or deceptive mortgage practices illegal with civil penalties, banned pre-dispute forced arbitration clauses in consumer contracts, and funded nonprofit borrower education. It never received a committee vote, let alone a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers in the subprime mortgage market — disproportionately lower-income families, older homeowners, and communities of color targeted by predatory lenders — would have gained certification standards, plain-language fee disclosure, penalties for deceptive practices, and the right to sue in court instead of being forced into arbitration.

how_it_helps.text: Requires HUD certification and testing for anyone providing subprime mortgage lending or brokerage services, covering federal lending laws and predatory practices, with decertification for violations [S2][S3].

Bars high-cost lenders and their agents from imposing any charge or fee that was not disclosed before the mortgage was signed, and requires plain-language disclosure of fees and of the borrower's rights [S2][S3].
Makes unfair or deceptive acts in providing subprime mortgage services unlawful, with civil penalties up to $10,000 per day for a first violation and $20,000 per day for repeat violations [S2][S3].

Declares unenforceable any pre-dispute forced arbitration clause in a consumer contract, restoring consumers' access to the courts, while still allowing arbitration if agreed to after a dispute arises [S2][S3].
Authorizes $1 million per year in grants to nonprofit community development corporations to educate borrowers and community groups about predatory lending [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Subprime mortgage lenders and brokers would face training, certification, disclosure, and penalty costs; creditors in consumer transactions generally would lose the forced arbitration clauses that lower their litigation exposure; and federal appropriations of $1 million per year would fund training and grants.
analysis.who_pays_short: Subprime mortgage lenders, brokers, and creditors

drawbacks.text: Certification and examination requirements could raise the cost of serving subprime borrowers and shrink the supply of credit to exactly the higher-risk borrowers the bill was meant to protect [S3].
The bill assigns overlapping rulemaking to HUD, the Federal Reserve, and the FTC, which could have produced slow or inconsistent enforcement across agencies [S3].
The $1 million annual funding for borrower education is small relative to the scale of the subprime market, so the education component alone would have had limited reach [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections — certified loan officers, no undisclosed fees, penalties for deception, and access to courts — would have meaningfully protected vulnerable borrowers from practices that later helped fuel the 2008 foreclosure crisis. The main honest cost is that certification rules could raise lenders' compliance costs and possibly tighten credit for some subprime borrowers; on balance the protections outweigh that risk, though the small education grants were modest in scale.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, sent to a subcommittee two months later, and sat there until the Congress ended, without ever coming up for a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Stephanie Tubbs Jones introduced the bill in the House on February 27, 2002 [S1][S5].
The House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services the same day [S5].
On April 15, 2002, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit; no markup, floor vote, or further action followed [S5].
The 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, so the bill died in committee without a vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Subprime mortgage lenders, mortgage brokers, and consumer-credit businesses that relied on forced arbitration clauses are better off, because none of the certification, fee-disclosure, or arbitration limits ever took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Subprime lenders and brokers, never regulated

for.name: Rep. Stephanie Tubbs Jones
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to certify subprime mortgage professionals, bar undisclosed fees, and ban forced arbitration in consumer contracts

for.name: 16 of 208 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Republicans did

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee on April 15, 2002 and never acted on it, so it died without a markup or vote

sides.party_line_note: All 16 cosponsors were House Democrats, and the bill never reached a floor vote in the chamber controlled by Republicans.

industries.note: The bill would have required certification and testing, banned undisclosed fees, and imposed daily civil penalties for deceptive practices, cutting into fee income and lending flexibility. Without the bill, the industry kept operating without these federal standards.

industries.industry: Consumer credit and financial services firms relying on forced arbitration
industries.note: The Consumer Fairness Act title would have made pre-dispute forced arbitration clauses unenforceable, letting consumers sue in court. Firms benefit from arbitration clauses because they limit class actions and litigation costs.
The bill authorized $1 million per year in grants for borrower education about predatory lending.
